title: A Coach's Dilemma
protagonist: Priya Shah, Houston Rockets analytics coordinator (fictional stand-in; the team, coach, players, games, and every statistic are real -- see case.json.origin and Appendix A)
replacement_note: This case fully replaces the previous 'A Coach's Dilemma' content (a fictionalized 2008 NCAA Championship scenario, legacy-converted 2026-08-13) at the project owner's explicit direction, after that content was found BLOCKED at Tier 2 QA on 2026-08-18 (Option B had no surviving quantitative footing once the required compound-probability step was worked, the Twist was pre-leaked in Appendix D, FACILITATOR.md quoted a case.md parenthetical that did not exist, and 2 of 3 cited sources did not support their claims -- see git history for the retired content and cases/a-coachs-dilemma/QA_REPORT.md for the original findings). The new content keeps the case id and title but is built from scratch on a real, documented, verifiable NBA scenario: the Houston Rockets' real 'Hack-a-Jordan' intentional-foul strategy against DeAndre Jordan in the real 2015 NBA Western Conference Semifinals. Every number is either cited to a real, fetched source or an explicit, disclosed Modeling Assumption (Appendix D) -- see RESEARCH_LOG.md for the full research trail, including what could NOT be cleanly sourced and why.
primary_metric: corrected expected points conceded by Houston per defensive possession (Hack-a-Jordan sequence vs. an ordinary defended Clippers possession), net of the two disclosed real-anchored costs of fouling: live-ball offensive-rebound risk after a missed second free throw, and Houston's own forfeited transition-offense value from stopping the clock

options.A: Recommend Hack-a-Jordan -- intentionally foul DeAndre Jordan away from the ball, all game
options.B: Recommend Play It Straight -- defend every Clippers possession honestly, no intentional fouls

reinforcement_note: Checked every claimed skill's n value in readmodel/standards_spine.json before writing (2026-08-18): none is n=0 -- advanced-numbers-percent (n=35), -decimal (n=30), the two how-tos (n=19, n=23), basic-operations-division/quotient (n=24, n=23), measurement-rounding/-how-to (n=30, n=29), number-sense-bar-graph (n=31), -how-to-compare-two-or-more-values (n=36), -place-value (n=2, already claimed by Cinema and Air Traffic Controller per the old case.json's own note), statistics-and-probability-probability/-event/-outcome (n=11/8/8), -dependent-event (n=2), -conditional-probability (n=2), -how-to-determine-the-probability-of-a-compound-event (n=3), -how-to-determine-the-probability-of-conditional-events (n=2). Checked the full n=0 list in the spine (dominated by geometry, pre-calculus, calculus, and discrete-math skills -- shortest-path in a weighted graph, conditional-statement logic, integration, series) for anything this case's real deliverables might naturally force instead of padding: nothing fits. This case's math is arithmetic-and-probability reinforcement (percent/decimal conversion on real makes-and-attempts data, a genuine compound/conditional-probability calculation for the live-ball-rebound risk in D3, and a foul-budget constraint calculation in D4) on skills the spine already has real coverage for -- an honest zero, not a fabricated one. D3's OREB-after-a-miss calculation genuinely forces conditional/dependent-event reasoning (the rebound chance is conditioned on the miss having occurred) distinct from the old case's independent-event p^2 mechanic, which is why statistics-and-probability-independent-event is NOT claimed here (this case never squares an independent probability) while -dependent-event and -conditional-probability are.

modeling_assumptions.text: Jordan's real season free-throw percentage (39.7%, Appendix B) is used as his single-attempt make probability for both attempts of an intentional foul. A real, standard simplifying convention that does not model game-to-game variance, defensive intensity, or fatigue -- deliberately, since predicting single-game variance in advance is not something this case's real, pre-game data can do (see FACILITATOR.md's Twist, which reveals what actually happened).

Extra expected points from a live-ball offensive rebound after Jordan misses his second free throw, valued at the Clippers' own real points-per-possession. Anchored to S5's real 10.4%-vs-24.7% estimate (nearest available public season, disclosed gap) and to S3's real Clippers points-per-possession as the value of a recovered live-ball possession. Derivation shown in case.md D3: (1 - 0.397) x 0.104 x 1.124 = ~0.07 points per intentional-foul sequence.

Transition-offense value Houston forfeits on its own next possession by intentionally fouling instead of forcing a live-ball stop. No single clean, dated, primary source specific to the 2014-15 season was found (see RESEARCH_LOG.md); several independent public estimates from this era place transition offense roughly 0.15-0.3 points per possession above half-court offense league-wide. This case uses the conservative low end of that real range (0.15) rather than an unsupported precise midpoint, applied only to Option A.

How much the Clippers' effective points-per-possession rises when Houston's primary center is off the floor (foul trouble or disqualified), replaced by a backup: a stated +8.0 points per 100 possessions (1.204 points per possession with the backup in). No clean, publicly available on/off defensive-rating split specific to this exact matchup was found (see RESEARCH_LOG.md). Reasoned from the well-established general real pattern -- documented across many NBA lineup studies broadly, though not pinned to this specific matchup -- that team defense measurably worsens when a primary rim-protecting big is replaced by a lesser one. Disclosed as a deliberately modest, arguable number, not a hidden fact.

deliverables.text: DeAndre Jordan's real free-throw percentages for the 2014-15 regular season and the Clippers' real first-round 2015 playoff series (Appendix B), computed from his real makes and attempts, each rounded to one decimal place -- plus the Clippers' real points scored per possession, computed from their real 2014-15 Offensive Rating (Appendix B).

A first-pass 'gut check' comparison: the expected points from two free throws at Jordan's real season free-throw percentage, versus the Clippers' real points-per-possession on an ordinary defended possession -- no adjustments yet.

A corrected expected-points comparison that starts from D2 and adds the two real, disclosed costs of fouling from Appendix D (the extra risk from a live-ball offensive rebound after a missed second free throw, and the transition-offense value forfeited by stopping the clock), with every step of the arithmetic shown.

A foul-budget calculation: using the real NBA six-foul disqualification rule and the fourth-quarter planning scenario in Appendix C, determine how many more intentional fouls Houston's primary center can absorb before disqualification, and recompute the Clippers' points-per-possession for the rest of the stretch using Appendix D's stated backup-center adjustment.

An original visual display (bar graph or equivalent) comparing the D2 'gut check,' D3 'corrected,' and D4 'roster-adjusted' expected-points figures for Hack-a-Jordan against Play It Straight's real points-per-possession baseline.

balance.argument_a: Even after Appendix D's two real, disclosed costs are added in (the live-ball-rebound risk and the transition-offense forfeit), fouling Jordan still comes out ahead on a pure expected-points-per-possession basis: ~1.01 points conceded per intentional-foul sequence versus the Clippers' real 1.124 points per ordinary possession -- a real, defensible ~9.7% edge for the foul, not a coin flip and not a blowout.
balance.argument_b: The corrected per-possession number in D3 never has to account for what fouling does to Houston's own roster durability. Every intentional foul is a real personal foul against Houston's primary rim-protecting center under the same real 6-foul rule that ends any player's night at foul #6. If he fouls out (D4), Houston finishes the stretch with a real, sourced, worse defender on the floor at Appendix D's stated backup-center cost (1.204 points per possession) -- a cost D3's per-possession number never has to pay, because Play It Straight accumulates fouls far more slowly. A coach who weighs that real structural risk, not just the per-possession average, has a fully legitimate, numbers-backed reason to choose B.
balance.margin_basis: D3's corrected expected-points comparison: 2 x 0.397 + 0.0705 (MA2) + 0.15 (MA3) = 1.0145 points conceded per Hack-a-Jordan sequence, versus the Clippers' real 1.124 points per ordinary possession (S3). Margin = (1.124 - 1.0145) / 1.124 = 9.74%, recorded as margin_pct 9.7. D4's roster-exhaustion risk is a real, disclosed, separate risk axis this per-possession metric does not capture -- it is the case's genuine second lever for Option B, not folded into the graded margin, exactly so Option B is never reduced to attacking the graded metric's own arithmetic (the defect the retired content had).
balance.stability: Not yet re-run under Tier 2 probe 5 for this content (this authoring pass ran Tier 1 self-check only, per explicit instruction not to run Tier 2). A hand check: removing MA3 (transition-suppression cost) entirely pushes the margin to (1.124-0.8645)/1.124 = 23.1%, which BREAKS the SPEC Section 2 20% cap -- meaning MA3 is load-bearing for balance, not decorative, and any future Tier 2 probe 5 run should flex it first. sensitivity_model.py implements a runnable version of this arithmetic for that future run.
